content: 1. Drugs excreted by glomerular filtration or active tubular secretion, including high-dose or multiple-dose NSAIDs, should be used cautiously. Alternatives to NSAIDs should be considered. Close monitoring is required when co-administering enalapril and aspirin, as they may increase each other's toxicity. This interaction is likely due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, which can lead to a significant reduction in renal function. NSAIDs may diminish the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors by reducing the synthesis of vasodilating renal prostaglandins. 2. Enoxaparin and aspirin both increase anticoagulation. When prescribed together for conditions such as unstable angina, non-Q-wave myocardial infarction (MI), or STEMI, additive effects are intended. However, close monitoring is necessary due to the risk of pharmacodynamic synergism, which can increase toxicity. 3. Aspirin increases serum potassium, while ephedrine decreases it. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, so caution and close monitoring are advised. 4. Aspirin increases serum potassium, while epinephrine (or racemic epinephrine) decreases it. The effect of this interaction is not well understood, and caution is recommended. 5. Aspirin decreases the effects of eplerenone through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction is minor, but monitoring is advised. NSAIDs, including aspirin, reduce prostaglandin synthesis, which may contribute to this effect. 6. Aspirin and epoprostenol both increase anticoagulation. Close monitoring is required to avoid excessive bleeding risk. 7. Aspirin decreases the effects of eprosartan through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Both drugs can increase serum potassium levels, and co-administration may lead to renal function deterioration, particularly in elderly or volume-depleted patients. Monitoring is essential. 8. Aspirin and eptifibatide both increase anticoagulation. This combination is common in cardiovascular disease management, but close monitoring is necessary due to the risk of pharmacodynamic synergism. 9. Aspirin and escitalopram increase the risk of upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. This is due to the inhibition of serotonin uptake by platelets caused by SSRIs. Caution and close monitoring are required. 10. Aspirin decreases the effects of esmolol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Long-term NSAID use may exacerbate this interaction. Both drugs can increase serum potassium levels, so monitoring is advised. 11. Aspirin increases serum potassium, while ethacrynic acid decreases it. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, so caution is recommended. 12. Ethanol increases the toxicity of aspirin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This combination increases the risk of GI bleeding. Monitoring is advised. 13. Aspirin and etodolac both increase anticoagulation and serum potassium levels. Aspirin may also increase the levels or effects of etodolac by competing for renal tubular clearance. Monitoring is recommended. 14. Aspirin and fenbufen both increase anticoagulation and serum potassium levels. Aspirin may increase the levels or effects of fenbufen through competition for renal tubular clearance. Monitoring is advised. 15. Aspirin and fennel both increase anticoagulation. Close monitoring is required to avoid excessive bleeding risk. 16. Aspirin and fenoprofen both increase anticoagulation and serum potassium levels. Aspirin may increase the levels or effects of fenoprofen through competition for renal tubular clearance. Monitoring is recommended. 17. Aspirin and feverfew both increase anticoagulation. However, aspirin may decrease the effects of feverfew through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitoring is advised. 18. Fish oil and aspirin both increase anticoagulation. Patients taking fish oil and anticoagulants or other drugs affecting coagulation should be monitored periodically due to the increased risk of bleeding. Prolonged bleeding has been reported in patients taking antiplatelet agents or anticoagulants with oral omega-3 fatty acids. 19. Aspirin and fludrocortisone may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Fludrocortisone may also decrease aspirin levels by increasing renal clearance. Monitoring is recommended. 20. Aspirin and fluoxetine increase the risk of upper GI bleeding. This is due to the inhibition of serotonin uptake by platelets caused by SSRIs. Close monitoring is required. 21. Aspirin and flurbiprofen both increase anticoagulation and serum potassium levels. Aspirin may increase the levels or effects of flurbiprofen through competition for renal tubular clearance. Monitoring is advised. 22. Aspirin and fluvoxamine increase the risk of upper GI bleeding. This is due to the inhibition of serotonin uptake by platelets caused by SSRIs. Monitoring is recommended. 23. Aspirin decreases folic acid levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Monitoring is advised. 24. Aspirin and fondaparinux both increase anticoagulation. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 25. Aspirin increases serum potassium, while formoterol decreases it. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, so caution is recommended. 26. Aspirin and forskolin both increase anticoagulation. Close monitoring is required to avoid excessive bleeding risk. 27. Aspirin and fosinopril may decrease renal function when co-administered. NSAIDs, including aspirin, may diminish the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors by reducing the synthesis of vasodilating renal prostaglandins. Therapy modification or alternative drugs should be considered. 28. Aspirin increases serum potassium, while furosemide decreases it. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, so caution is recommended. Aspirin may also decrease the effects of furosemide through pharmacodynamic antagonism. 29. Aspirin may increase the levels or effects of ganciclovir through competition for renal tubular clearance. Monitoring is advised. 30. Aspirin and garlic both increase anticoagulation. Close monitoring is required to avoid excessive bleeding risk.
